lessons.title: Greeting and Engaging Customers in a Friendly Way
lessons.body:
When a customer walks into your thrift shop, the first 10 seconds decide whether they stay or leave. In many African markets, a warm greeting is expected. Start with a smile and a simple "Welcome! How are you today?" in the local language if possible. For example, in Nigeria, say "Sannu da zuwa" in Hausa, "Nná»á»" in Igbo, or "áº¸ kÃ¡Ã bá»Ì" in Yoruba. This instantly makes people feel at home.

Don't just stand behind your pile of clothes. Move around, arrange items, and greet each person who enters. If you're busy with another customer, acknowledge the new one with eye contact and a nod. Say, "I'll be with you in a moment." This prevents them from feeling ignored. In a busy market like Balogun in Lagos or Kantamanto in Accra, a friendly face stands out.

Ask open-ended questions to start a conversation. Instead of "Can I help you?" which often gets a "No," try "Are you looking for something specific today?" or "We just got new jeans and dressesâwould you like to see?" If they say they're just browsing, respond with "Take your time. Let me know if you need anything." Then give them space but stay nearby.

Use compliments genuinely. If a customer tries on a shirt, say "That colour looks great on you!" But don't overdo itâpeople can tell when you're just flattering. Also, be mindful of personal space and cultural norms. In some cultures, direct eye contact is respectful; in others, it's not. Observe and adapt.

Finally, always thank them for coming, even if they don't buy. Say, "Thank you for stopping by. Please come again." A polite exit leaves the door open for a future sale. Remember, in the okrika business, word travels fast. A friendly greeting can turn a one-time visitor into a regular customer who tells others about your shop.

lessons.title: Handling Bargaining and Negotiation Tactics
lessons.body:
In African markets, bargaining is normal. If you don't expect it, you'll get frustrated. The key is to set your prices with bargaining in mind. For example, if you want to sell a shirt for 500 naira, price it at 800 naira. That way, when a customer offers 400, you can meet at 500 or 550. Never start with your lowest price.

When a customer asks for a discount, don't say yes immediately. Instead, ask, "How much do you want to pay?" Let them make the first offer. If they say 300 for a 800 naira item, counter with 700. Then go back and forth. Use phrases like "I can't go that low, but I can do 600" or "If you buy two, I'll give you a better price." This shifts the focus to volume.

Stay calm and friendly. Never argue or insult. If a customer offers too little, smile and say, "That price is too low for me. But I can give you a small discount if you pay cash now." Cash is kingâoffer 5-10% off for immediate payment. Also, use the "good cop, bad cop" trick: pretend to call your boss or partner and say, "My boss says I can only go down to 550." This makes the discount seem like a favour.

Know your bottom line. Before you start, decide the lowest price you'll accept. If a customer won't meet it, politely say, "I'm sorry, I can't sell at that price. But I have similar items for less." Then show them a cheaper alternative. This keeps the sale alive.

Finally, don't be afraid to walk away. Sometimes a customer will chase after you and agree to your price. But if they don't, it's okay. There will be other buyers. Remember, bargaining is a game. The more you practice, the better you'll get. And always keep a calculator or phone handy to do quick math.

lessons.title: Upselling and Cross-Selling Accessories
lessons.body:
Upselling means convincing a customer to buy a more expensive item or add something extra. Cross-selling means suggesting related products. In the okrika business, this can increase your sales by 30-50% if done right. For example, if someone buys a dress, ask, "Would you like a belt or a handbag to go with that?" If they buy a shirt, say, "We have matching trousers for just 300 naira more."

Start by knowing your inventory. Group items togetherâshoes with bags, belts with jeans, jewellery with dresses. When a customer shows interest in one item, immediately think of what else they might need. Use phrases like "This would look great with..." or "Customers who bought this also loved..." Keep it natural, not pushy.

Offer bundles at a discount. For example, "Buy a top and a skirt for 1,000 naira instead of 1,200." Or "Get a free scarf when you spend 2,000 naira." This encourages larger purchases. In many African markets, people love a bargain, so bundles work well.

Timing is important. Don't suggest extras before the customer has decided on the main item. Wait until they seem interested or are about to pay. Then say, "By the way, we have a special on accessories today." If they say no, don't push. Just smile and say, "No problem. Maybe next time."

Train your helpers or family members to do the same. If you have a stall, have one person at the till and another on the floor suggesting add-ons. Also, place small, cheap items near the counterâsocks, hair ties, phone cases. These are easy impulse buys. For example, a customer paying for a shirt might grab a 100 naira pair of socks. Over a day, that adds up.

Finally, track what works. Note which add-ons sell best. If belts are popular, stock more. If no one buys hats, stop suggesting them. Adjust your strategy based on what customers actually buy.

lessons.title: Dealing with Difficult Customers and Returns
lessons.body:
In any business, you'll meet difficult customers. They may be rude, impatient, or accuse you of cheating. In the okrika business, returns are common because items are second-hand. The key is to stay calm and professional. Never argue or raise your voice. Listen to their complaint, then repeat it back: "So you're saying the shirt has a tear that I didn't show you?" This shows you're paying attention.

If a customer wants to return an item, have a clear policy. For example, "Returns are accepted within 3 days if the item is unworn and tags are attached." But since okrika often has no tags, you might say, "Exchanges only, and only if the item is defective." Write this on a small sign or tell customers when they buy. If they didn't know, be flexible. A one-time exchange can keep a customer happy.

When a customer is angry, don't take it personally. They might be having a bad day. Offer a solution: "I can't give you a refund, but I can exchange it for something else of the same value." If they refuse, ask, "What would make you happy?" Sometimes they just want to be heard. If they become abusive, politely ask them to leave. You don't have to tolerate insults.

For difficult hagglers who won't accept your price, stay firm but polite. Say, "I understand, but this is my final price. If you change your mind, I'm here." Then turn to another customer. This shows you're not desperate.

Document any return or exchange in a notebook. Write the date, item, and reason. This helps you spot patternsâmaybe a supplier sells you defective goods. Also, train your staff to handle complaints the same way. A consistent policy builds trust. Remember, a difficult customer handled well can become your best promoter. They'll tell others how fair you were.

lessons.title: Building Repeat Business and Referrals
lessons.body:
Getting a new customer costs more than keeping an old one. In the thrift business, repeat customers are your lifeline. To build loyalty, start by remembering names and preferences. If Mama Ngozi always buys size 12 dresses, set them aside when new stock arrives. Call her and say, "I found something you'll love." This personal touch makes her feel special.

Offer a loyalty program. For example, after 5 purchases, give a 10% discount or a free item. You can use a simple card and punch a hole each time. Or keep a notebook with customer names and purchases. In many African markets, a small gift goes a long wayâa free scarf or a pair of socks. It shows you appreciate them.

Ask for referrals. After a good sale, say, "If you have friends who love thrift shopping, please tell them about us. If they mention your name, you'll get 5% off your next buy." Word of mouth is powerful. In tight-knit communities, one happy customer can bring ten more.

Stay in touch. If you have a phone, collect WhatsApp numbers (with permission). Send a message when you get new stock: "New arrivals just in! Come see." But don't spamâonce a week is enough. You can also create a WhatsApp group for your best customers. Post photos of items and prices. This makes buying easy.

Be consistent. Open your shop at the same time every day. Keep your prices fair. If you promise to hold an item, do it. Trust is everything. If you're ever out of stock, offer to order something similar. This shows you care about their needs.

Finally, thank your regulars. A simple "Thank you for your support" goes a long way. Happy customers not only return but also defend your business if others complain. They become your unpaid sales team.

lessons.title: Managing Crowds During Peak Hours
lessons.body:
Peak hours in a thrift shop can be hecticâweekends, month-end, or after new stock arrives. Without a plan, you'll lose sales and customers. Start by preparing ahead. Before the rush, arrange items neatly, restock popular sizes, and have extra bags and change ready. If you have helpers, assign roles: one at the entrance to greet, one on the floor to assist, one at the till.

Create a simple queue system. Use a rope or a line of chairs to guide customers. If your shop is small, ask customers to form a line outside. In busy markets like Katwe in Kampala, sellers use a "one in, one out" rule to avoid overcrowding. But be friendlyâsay "Please wait, we'll call you in shortly."

Keep an eye on security. Crowds attract thieves. Have a helper watch for suspicious behaviour. Keep expensive items behind the counter. If you see someone stealing, don't confront them alone. Politely say, "Excuse me, did you need help with that?" and guide them to the till. If they run, don't chaseâyour safety first.

Speed up transactions. Use a calculator or phone to add prices quickly. If you have a mobile money account, have the QR code ready. For cash, keep small notes and coins accessible. Bag items as you go. If lines get too long, open a second till if possible.

Manage your energy. Peak hours can last 3-4 hours. Drink water, take short breaks if you can. Don't snap at customersâstress is contagious. If you feel overwhelmed, take a deep breath and focus on one customer at a time.

After the rush, take 15 minutes to tidy up and note what sold out. This helps you restock for next time. Also, thank your customers for their patience. A calm, organised shop during peak hours builds a reputation for good service, and customers will come back even when it's busy.

quiz.q: What is the best way to greet a customer in a thrift shop?
options: A) Ignore them until they ask for help
B) Smile and say 'Welcome! How are you today?'
D) Stay behind the counter and wait
quiz.explanation: A warm, friendly greeting makes customers feel welcome and more likely to stay.

quiz.q: Why should you price an item higher than your desired selling price?
options: B) To leave room for bargaining
quiz.explanation: In bargaining cultures, starting high allows you to negotiate down to your target price.

quiz.q: What is upselling?
options: B) Convincing a customer to buy a more expensive item or add-on
C) Selling to a customer standing up
quiz.explanation: Upselling encourages customers to spend more by upgrading or adding items.

quiz.q: How should you handle a customer who wants to return a defective item?
options: B) Offer an exchange or store credit
quiz.explanation: A fair exchange or credit keeps the customer happy and maintains your reputation.

quiz.q: What is a good way to build repeat business?
options: A) Remember customer names and preferences
quiz.explanation: Personal attention makes customers feel valued and encourages them to return.

quiz.q: During peak hours, what should you do to manage crowds?
options: B) Create a queue system and assign roles to helpers
C) Serve only one customer at a time
quiz.explanation: Organisation and teamwork help you serve more customers efficiently.

quiz.q: What is a good phrase to use when a customer says they are just browsing?
options: B) 'Take your time. Let me know if you need anything.'
quiz.explanation: This response is polite and gives the customer space while keeping the door open.

quiz.q: Why is it important to know your bottom line in bargaining?
options: A) To avoid selling at a loss
quiz.explanation: Knowing your lowest acceptable price prevents you from making unprofitable deals.

quiz.q: What is cross-selling?
options: B) Suggesting related products to a customer
C) Selling to two customers at once
quiz.explanation: Cross-selling means recommending complementary items to increase the sale.

quiz.q: How can you handle a difficult customer who is shouting?
options: B) Stay calm and listen to their complaint
quiz.explanation: Staying calm and listening helps de-escalate the situation and find a solution.

quiz.q: What is a simple loyalty program for a thrift shop?
options: A) Give a free item after 5 purchases
quiz.explanation: Rewarding repeat purchases encourages customers to keep coming back.

quiz.q: Why should you have a helper watch for thieves during peak hours?
options: A) To catch them and beat them
B) To prevent theft and keep your business safe
quiz.explanation: Security during busy times protects your stock and profits.

quiz.q: What is a good way to start a conversation with a customer?
options: B) 'Are you looking for something specific today?'
quiz.explanation: Open-ended questions engage customers and help you understand their needs.

quiz.q: When is the best time to offer an upsell?
options: A) Before the customer shows interest
B) After they have decided on a main item
quiz.explanation: Timing the upsell after the main decision increases the chance of an additional sale.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer becomes abusive?
options: A) Politely ask them to leave
quiz.explanation: You have the right to refuse service to abusive customers and protect yourself.

quiz.q: How can you encourage referrals?
options: A) Offer a discount to customers who refer friends
B) Tell customers to bring friends or else
C) Only serve people you know
quiz.explanation: Incentives like discounts motivate customers to spread the word.

quiz.q: What is a good way to manage a queue during peak hours?
options: A) Use a rope or chairs to form a line
quiz.explanation: A physical queue system keeps order and ensures fair service.

quiz.q: Why should you document returns and exchanges?
options: A) To track patterns and improve your stock
B) To report customers to the police
quiz.explanation: Records help you identify faulty suppliers or common issues and adjust your business.

quiz.q: What is a good way to stay in touch with customers?
options: A) Send WhatsApp messages about new stock
quiz.explanation: A weekly WhatsApp update is a respectful way to remind customers of your shop.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see someone stealing?
options: B) Politely offer help and guide them to the till
quiz.explanation: A polite approach can defuse the situation without risking your safety.

quiz.q: Why is cash payment often rewarded with a discount?
options: A) Cash is immediate and avoids mobile money fees
C) Cash is easier to steal
quiz.explanation: Cash provides instant funds and reduces transaction costs, so you can share the benefit.

quiz.q: What is a good way to handle a customer who offers too little for an item?
options: B) Counter with a higher price and stay firm
quiz.explanation: Countering and staying firm shows you value your goods and encourages a fair price.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of bundling items?
options: A) It increases the total sale and moves slow stock
quiz.explanation: Bundles encourage larger purchases and help clear inventory.

quiz.q: How can you make a customer feel special?
options: A) Remember their name and preferences
quiz.explanation: Personal recognition builds loyalty and repeat business.

quiz.q: What should you do after a peak hour rush?
options: A) Tidy up and note what sold out
B) Close the shop for the day
quiz.explanation: Restocking and reviewing sales helps you prepare for the next busy period.

quiz.q: Why is it important to thank customers even if they don't buy?
options: A) It leaves a good impression and encourages them to return
C) It makes them feel guilty
quiz.explanation: Politeness costs nothing and can turn a browser into a future buyer.

quiz.q: What is a good way to handle a customer who wants a refund but you have a no-refund policy?
options: A) Offer an exchange or credit note
quiz.explanation: An exchange or credit keeps the customer satisfied without breaking your policy.

quiz.q: How can you speed up transactions during peak hours?
options: A) Use a calculator and have change ready
B) Chat with each customer for 10 minutes
quiz.explanation: Preparation and quick math reduce waiting times and keep the line moving.

quiz.q: What is a good way to encourage customers to buy more?
options: A) Offer a discount for buying two or more items
D) Serve only one customer at a time
quiz.explanation: Volume discounts motivate customers to purchase more than they planned.

quiz.q: Why should you stay calm when a customer is angry?
options: A) It helps you think clearly and resolve the issue
B) It shows you are weak
quiz.explanation: Calmness de-escalates conflict and allows you to find a fair solution.
